titre: An Assassinated Mediator and the Legal Personality of the UN
accroche: In 1948, a UN mediator is killed in Jerusalem. Nearly seven months later, the Hague Court says whether the Organization can itself claim reparation.
contenu_vulgarise:
On September 17, 1948, in Jerusalem, Count Folke Bernadotte, the United Nations Mediator for Palestine, is killed when his convoy is ambushed. French Colonel André Sérot, who is traveling with him, dies with him. The Organization is not yet three years old. One of its agents has just been killed in the performance of his mission, and a legal question arises: can it, as a State would for one of its diplomats, claim reparation from the responsible government?

## A Question the Charter Does Not Settle

On December 3, 1948, the General Assembly puts the question to the International Court of Justice. Does the UN have the capacity to bring an international claim against the responsible government, first for the damage caused to the Organization itself, and second for that caused to the victim or those entitled through him? And if so, how is this action to be reconciled with the rights of the State of which the victim is a national?

The difficulty is one of principle. The Charter of the United Nations (1945) does not say in so many words that the Organization possesses international personality: the Court itself notes that the question is not settled by the terms of the Charter.

## The Court's Reasoning

On April 11, 1949, it answers yes. It reasons from the functions entrusted to the Organization. In its view, the Organization must be regarded as having those powers which, though not expressly provided in the Charter, are conferred upon it by necessary implication as being essential to the performance of its duties. The subjects of law in any legal system are not necessarily identical, it adds, either in their nature or in the extent of their rights. A State possesses the totality of international rights and duties recognized by international law, whereas those of an organization depend on its purposes and functions, as specified or implied in its constituent documents and developed in practice.

There remains the case of States that did not found the UN. The Court dismisses the objection: fifty States, representing the vast majority of the members of the international community, had the power to bring into being an entity possessing objective international personality, and not merely personality recognized by them alone. The first branch, damage suffered by the Organization, is decided unanimously. The second, damage suffered by the victim, passes by eleven votes to four. On how this fits with the victim's State of nationality, the vote is ten to five.

## What This Shifts

The opinion does not concern mediators alone: it covers the agents of the Organization in general. It establishes that a subject of international law can be something other than a State, and that its rights are deduced from its task rather than from a list. How far can an organization extend what its founders did not write?

repere.texte: April 11, 1949: the International Court of Justice recognizes the UN's capacity to claim reparation for the damage suffered by the Organization (unanimously) and for that suffered by the victim (eleven votes to four).
repere.source: International Court of Justice, Advisory Opinion of April 11, 1949, Reparation for Injuries Suffered in the Service of the United Nations, I.C.J. Reports 1949

carte.punch: A mediator killed in 1948: the Court decides the UN can itself claim reparation.
carte.idee: On April 11, 1949, after Count Bernadotte's assassination, the International Court of Justice rules that the UN possesses international personality, even though the Charter does not write it: an organization has the powers its functions make necessary.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: The case page at the ICJ (opinion, summary, judges' opinions)
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Gives access to the opinion in English and French and to the separate or dissenting opinions.

quiz.question: On what does the Court base, in 1949, the UN's capacity to claim reparation?
choix: On an article of the Charter that expressly grants the UN international legal personality
On a separate treaty, concluded after Bernadotte's death and later signed by all States
On the individual recognition of each State, the UN having rights only against those that recognized it
On its functions: the Organization has the powers necessary for the mission entrusted to it
quiz.explication: The Court notes that the Charter does not settle the question in so many words and deduces the capacity from the functions entrusted to the Organization. It also holds that fifty States could create an objective personality, not merely one recognized by them, which rules out the UN having rights only against those that recognized it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who was killed with Count Bernadotte in the ambush of September 17, 1948?
choix: The Secretary-General of the United Nations
quiz_supplementaire.explication: French Colonel André Sérot, who was traveling with Bernadotte in his convoy in Jerusalem, dies with him in the ambush.

quiz_supplementaire.question: By how many votes does the Court recognize the UN's capacity to claim reparation for the damage suffered by the Organization itself?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The first branch, damage suffered by the Organization itself, is decided unanimously; the second, damage suffered by the victim, by eleven votes to four.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does the Court answer the objection of States that did not found the UN?
choix: It grants them a veto over any claim by the Organization
It holds that fifty States could create an entity with objective international personality
It requires these States to ratify the Charter before any claim
It declines to rule on this objection, for lack of a sufficient majority
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Court dismisses the objection: fifty States, representing the vast majority of the international community, had the power to bring into being an objective international personality.
